In all milk porridge, honey should be placed on top; in all curd, granulated sugar should be added; and in the bean soup, cow's ghee should be placed, and if there is ginger, that too should be added.
"Furthermore, one should offer various kinds of fruits and roots as food; these two types of food—fruits and roots—are beloved by all mantras as well as the Vidyā-deities."

"As for those fruits, they include the *āmra* fruit, pomegranate fruit, *mālūka* fruit, grapes, jujube, persimmon, *kapittha* fruit, *viśālapuṣpaka* fruit, walnut, *panasa* fruit, *tinduka* fruit, *laṅkuja* fruit, *mucukunda* fruit, wood-apple, *pārāvataka* fruit, *kṛsara* fruit, *āmra* fruit, *campaka* fruit, *mṛdvīkā* fruit, *kāramardaka* fruit, and so forth—various excellent fruits used for making offerings."
All foul-smelling fruits should not be offered. As for those considered foul fruits: the śrīphala fruit, coconut, tāla fruit, pāṭala fruit... such foul fruits as these should not be offered.

"One should also make offerings of various root medicines; having boiled them thoroughly and removed their skins, one should present them as offerings according to the Dharma, such as the roots of *vitara* and the roots of taro, and so forth."

Those with foul roots should not be offered as oblations; those with foul roots refer to the śūlana root, the radish root, the karkandhu-gandha root, and so forth—such foul roots should not be offered as oblations.
"Among fruits, the pomegranate is supreme;
among roots, the vidula root is supreme.
Therefore, one should select these specifically to use for making offerings."
One should offer it by boiling small beans until they are soft, mixing them with beef ghee and adding sesame seeds.
"In the third maṇḍala, one should scatter white flowers upon the ground around the four outer sides, and likewise scatter sesame seeds and rice blossoms everywhere."

"Finally, when going outside, one should perform sacrifices to the bhūtas and various non-human beings in all directions, using cooked rice of *śāli* paddy mixed with *taṇḍula* (rice powder), sesame, and flowers; boiled mung beans; and *sāyali-ka* rice mixed with clarified butter (*ghee*). All these offerings should be combined into a single place."

"With a joyful heart, that ācārya shall offer food three times in each of the directions to worship the rākṣasas, piśācas, and various classes of bhūtas who consume blood and flesh; whether they dwell upon the earth, in trees, or in forests, or those to whom his mind is devoted, all must be worshipped."
"At that time, if suddenly a great sound is heard, one should perform the sacrifice again with a fearless mind;

or if the loud howling of a jackal or the roar of a great beast is heard; or if its body is seen; or if the roots of uprooted trees are seen, or trees are seen broken; or if the sound of thunder is heard, or various rare and extraordinary omens appear—one should once more perform the sacrifice to provide protection for the body."

"Once that ācārya has performed the offerings in all directions according to what he has heard, understood, seen, and in accordance with the Dharma, he shall wash his hands, perform the ritual sprinkling for purification, and offer incense as an offering before the gate."

Next, enter within and offer argha water and incense, making offerings of the food previously set out. With the mind, extend these offerings to all the deities in the second and third courtyards, presenting each with exquisite, new, and pure garments; for all the other deities, present one length of cloth each.

Alternatively, if one cannot distinguish [the specific deities], one may offer two pieces of cloth each to the principal deity of each of the three families; or, simply placing two pieces of cloth inside a casket, one may offer them to the inner court while mentally dedicating the gift universally to all the honored ones.

Thereafter, one should recite the mantras of each deity seven times; for the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord, one should recite it more than one hundred times; for the heart-mantras of the three families, one should recite each one hundred times; thereafter, one should sequentially perform the individual mudrās of each deity, reciting them three times each.
Having performed this, all were filled with joy, their wishes being fulfilled.
At the end of the middle fascicle of the *Rahasya-sūtra*, the Lingyun edition notes:

"The collation was completed on the eleventh day of the sixth month in the third year of the Zhenheng era, the Bingyin year. This was done because [the text] was to be bestowed upon the fellow practitioners of Chan the following day."
The Bhikṣu Jingyan of Henan, who has practiced the Dharma for forty-eight years,
[translates] the *Rahasya-sūtra*, Volume II.
Compiled at the Great Xingshan Monastery during the Great Tang Dynasty by the Grand Master of State Affairs (Kaifu Yitongs).
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master, the Minister of State for the Reception of Guests (Shi Honglu Qing), by Imperial Decree. Chapter Nine:

Distinguishing the Characteristics (*Vibhaktalakṣaṇa*) Also known as the "Samaya Seals of the Three Sections," these are seals universally applicable to all maṇḍalas. These include: the seal for protecting the body; the seal for binding the directions; the seal for awakening and welcoming [the deities]; the seal for empowerment (*abhiṣeka*); the seal for warding off obstacles and difficulties; the seals for offering incense and flowers; the seal for pacifying calamities and difficulties; the seal for crushing and subduing difficulties; the seal for binding difficulties; and the seal for releasing difficulties... such seals as these are all explained in detail within the Chapter on Hand-Seals (*Mudrā-paṭala*).
The methods for purifying and protecting the body as previously described are all to be performed in conjunction with hand gestures (*mudrā*).
If one wishes to crush and subdue those who are difficult to subdue, one should employ the *Vajramātṛkā* mudrā, as well as all eighteen great mudrās taught within the Secret Maṇḍala;
if performing the rite of summoning, one should employ the *Vajrāṅkuśa* (Vajra Hook) mudrā.
If one performs the rite of binding, one should employ the Vajra-shṛṅkhala mudrā;
if one performs the rite of subjugation, one should employ the Vajra-daṇḍa mudrā;
if one performs the rite of terrifying, one should employ the Vajra-bhakṣaṇa mudrā.
If there should be anyone who transgresses the samaya, one should employ the wrathful mudrā for receiving the samaya to subdue them, or else the mudrā of the Great Power Vajra Staff;
if one wishes to shatter and destroy all obstacles and difficulties, one should employ the mantra and hand-mudrā of the Sovereign Mantra King Sunbha.
Once this rite has been performed, all such obstacles and difficulties will be consumed by fire.
Therefore, one should employ the aforementioned methods of the various seals (*mudrā*) and so forth as a protective circumambulation; thus one will know that there is great majestic power.
Therefore, one should employ all matters accordingly, or follow what has been taught and apply them to those ends.
Furthermore, one should perform the rite of homa:
facing the east, sitting upon the tips of *kuśa* grass, having kindled the fire until it is well-established, one sprinkles water to purify the fire.

Furthermore, using *kuśa* grass, one should first perform the homa with a full ladle of clarified butter (*sarpis*), and likewise at the end; thereafter, one should perform the homa according to the ritual rules with clarified butter, firewood, and other materials.
As with the method for recitation, so it is with the homa.

One should perform seven homa offerings for each deity using the śāntika mantra while mentally focusing on that deity. Once the homa for one deity is completed, one must immediately purify the fire before performing the homa for the next deity.

"Once the homa is completed, invite all the honored deities once more and perform homa one hundred and eight times. Then, seek the favor and joy of the honored deities, confess all karmic obstacles, rejoice in all merit, make vast aspirations, repeatedly take refuge in the Triple Gem, and take refuge in the assembly of non-regressive great bodhisattvas and all vidyā-mantras along with the vidyā-deities. Furthermore, repeatedly arouse the great bodhicitta."

"Next, one should praise the deities of the three families and all other deities; then, one should recite the sūtras. Thereafter, with a sincere heart, one should entreat the deities, generating a profound sense of reverence. One must ensure that the incense being burned does not cease and should repeatedly offer argha water."

"Having completed the ritual procedures in this sequential order, one should again prostrate with a sincere heart to all the Honored Ones, and then, according to the Dharma, lead each disciple into [the mandala] one by one."

One should call each disciple individually, purify them by sprinkling the aforementioned scented water, and offer them incense and other offerings. Then, having applied fragrance to one's own hands, one should press them upon the disciple's heart while reciting their respective mantra.
Next, recite the *Vastuvicaya-mantra* over a new piece of cloth and tie it around the face.
Then, form the *Samaya-mudrā*, place it upon the crown of the head, and recite that mantra three times.
Next, form the mudrā of the Maṇḍala Lord and place it upon the crown of the head; recite its mantra three times and lead [the disciple] to the entrance of the maṇḍala.
The Ācārya should speak as follows:

"We, such-and-such [names], have constructed this maṇḍala according to the Dharma and shall now lead the disciples inside. In accordance with their merit, their lineage, their accomplishments, and their capacity as vessels for the Dharma, we pray that you will observe their signs within this maṇḍala."
Next, one should scatter flowers; wherever they fall, that [disciple] belongs to that particular family clan and honored deity.
Next, one should uncover their face and have them look upon the maṇḍala. With a joyful heart, the ācārya should speak these words to the disciple:
"Now you behold this wondrous maṇḍala and give rise to deep reverence and faith; you have now entered the household of all the Buddhas."
All vidyā-mantras have now been bestowed upon you; may all auspiciousness and accomplishments manifest before you.
Therefore, firmly maintain the samaya precepts and apply yourself diligently to the recitation of mantras within this dharma.
Next, have the disciple universally offer incense, flowers, and so forth to the three families, and praise them.

The ācārya shall bestow upon the disciple at the maṇḍala whatever he has obtained from his own root mantra; or, having the disciple sit in the second enclosure, he shall cause him to recite the heart-mantra he has obtained. He must carefully observe the scattered flowers and determine the superior, middling, or inferior accomplishment according to where they fall—namely, by inferring the superiority or inferiority based on the distinctions of rank among the deities and the order of their seating positions.
If a flower falls upon the Buddha’s head, one should know that the mantras of the Buddha-uṣṇīṣa and the mantras of various deities such as the Buddha-ūrṇā have been accomplished;
if a flower falls upon the Buddha’s face, one should know that the vidyā-mantras of deities such as Buddhalocanā have been accomplished;
if a flower falls upon the Buddha’s central parts of the body, one should know that the various hṛdaya-mantras have been accomplished.
If the flower falls upon the lower part of the Buddha’s body, one should know that the mantra of the messenger will be accomplished.
According to where the flower falls—upon the upper, middle, or lower parts of the body—one should know that the accomplishment will be of the superior, middling, or inferior grade.
As for those holding lotuses or vajras, it should be understood according to the aforementioned method based on where the flower falls;
as for all other deities, one need only know the superior, middling, and inferior grades of accomplishment.
"If the flower falls at a distance from a deity, one should know that accomplishment will only be achieved after a long time.
If the flower falls upon the food court, one obtains the mantra of whichever deity it belongs to;
if the flower falls between two deities, one obtains the mantra of whichever is closer."

If the flower first falls within the inner enclosure and then passes out again through the outer enclosure, one should know that such a person lacks faith; if they nevertheless persist in recitation, they will obtain only inferior accomplishment.
If the flower falls upon the boundary paths or the circumambulation courtyards, one should know that this person lacks a resolute mind and will not attain accomplishment.

If the flower falls between the two deities—neither too near nor too far—or if it falls on a boundary path or a circumambulation courtyard, and one wishes to cast it again, one should perform the homa rite for that person and only then cast the flower.

"If the flower falls within an inner court, it belongs to whichever deity presides over that court. In constructing a maṇḍala, one should place the deities of the three families; furthermore, one should set up an additional seat in its own direction to represent the deities of a single family through the application of the mind."
Within the inner courtyard, one must further place a copy of the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra; at the gate of the inner courtyard, one must necessarily station the Dragon King who Guards the Central Gate.
If the flower falls upon the food-offering court, one should know that rites of enrichment (*puṣṭi*) and so forth will be accomplished;
if the flower falls upon the principal deity of the family, one should know that the accomplishment of the maṇḍala will be achieved.
If the flower falls upon the bodies of the Seven World-Honored Buddhas, one will certainly achieve the mantras of the three families;
if it falls upon the Holder of the Lotus, know that one will achieve the mantras of two families;
if it falls upon the Holder of the Vajra, know that one will achieve the mantra of one's own family.

"If the flower first falls within the third enclosure but then passes out over the path of the courtyard, that person should be discarded; at a later time, they shall be admitted into another maṇḍala."
If one wishes to force them to enter, one should perform a *homa* and have them cast flowers once more.
If they still do not land [on the mandala], perform the *homa* again.
If after three such attempts they still do not land, they must be expelled.

"The Ācārya, by means of this rite, shall lead each of the disciples in turn into [the mandala]. Once the scattering of flowers is complete, they shall again offer arghya water, incense, flowers, and so forth; then each disciple should likewise provide a gift."

The Ācārya shall then lead each disciple one by one to sit to the left of the Ācārya at the site of the homa. The Ācārya should take the disciple’s right thumb with his left hand and perform seven homa offerings of cow-ghee using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord; then, perform seven more homa offerings of cow-ghee using the Śāntika mantra. Next, he should perform three clockwise circumambulations around the disciple’s head while offering cow-ghee. Then, he should tie a divine pouch (devapuṭaka) upon the disciple’s right shoulder, apply fragrant paste to his hands and press them against the disciple’s chest, and finally, after reciting as desired, dismiss the disciple.
All other disciples should likewise perform the homa in this manner. One should perform the homa of clarified butter using a sruva ladle.

Furthermore, one should perform the homa of various grains with the right hand while seated upon a seat of *kuśa* grass. One should also place *kuśa* grass within the pure water; first prepare a circle of *kuśa* grass, and further spread *kuśa* grass on all four sides of the hearth. When performing the homa, it should be done in this way for all.
First, take milk and dry firewood and place them in the hearth; sprinkle clarified butter (sarpis) over them to ignite the fire, and afterwards perform the homa with milk and moist wood.
Just as the number of oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) varies according to the count, so too does the quantity of sesame seeds.
Other grains and such may be offered by oblation according to one's inclination, concluding finally with an oblation of full clarified butter.

"The mantras used for inviting the fire deity and for dismissal are those previously mentioned; the mantras used for sprinkling purification (prokṣaṇa) and so forth are also those previously mentioned, or one may follow other teachings. If there are specific mantras prescribed for use in the homa, they may be employed according to one's preference."

Chapter Ten: The Classification of Homa, from the *Guhya-tantra*. Next, the distinct methods for the three types of homa—pacifying (*śāntika*), increasing (*paustika*), and subjugating (*abhicāruka*)—will be explained. Having constructed the mandala accordingly, one should perform the homa according to the specific purpose.
"If one performs the śāntika homa, one should sit facing north;
if one performs the pauṣṭika homa, one should sit facing east;
if one performs the ābhicāruka homa, one should sit facing south."
"If one performs the śāntika maṇḍala and homa, the hearth should be made circular;
if for pauṣṭika, square; if for abhicāruka, triangular."
"If one performs the śāntika maṇḍala and homa, one should use white;
for pauṣṭika, yellow; and for vaśīkaraṇa, black."
"If one performs the rite of pacification (śāntika), one should sit upon a lotus seat;
for the rite of enrichment (pauṣṭika), one sits upon a grass seat;
for the rite of subjugation (abhicāruka), one crouches with the right foot pressing down upon the left, not sitting directly on the ground."

"Perform the rite of pacification with a mind of tranquility; perform the rite of augmentation with a mind of joy; perform the rite of subjugation with a mind of wrath; or perform them according to what is taught in the specific root-text."
"If one performs the rite of pacification (śāntika), one should perform homa using the highest branch of a tree;
if one performs the rite of enrichment (pauṣṭika), one should perform homa using the middle branch of a tree;
if one performs the rite of subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa)..."
One should perform the homa using tree roots.
If performing a rite for pacification (śāntika), one should wear a garment of *kuśa* grass;
if performing a rite for augmentation (pauṣṭika), one should wear a garment of *śaṇa* hemp.
If one performs rites of subjugation (*abhicāra*), one should wear blue garments, or blood-stained wet clothes, or tattered and filthy rags, or even go naked.

If one performs rites for the pacification of calamities (*śāntika*), one should perform *homa* using ghee, milk, rice blossoms, barley, honey, milk porridge, sprouts of *kuśa* grass, along with *kubjaka* flowers, leaves of the *nudatru* tree, white sandalwood, *udumbara* wood and its fruit, *aśvattha* wood, *khadira* wood, fruits of the *śamī* tree, *pārijāta* wood, and various other such substances.

If one performs rites for augmentation (puṣṭika), one should perform homa with milk porridge, curd-rice, honey-milk, as well as rice, curd, gruel, sesame, the "three white foods," celestial wood (devadāru), fennel (yavānī), celestial gate (devadvāra), winter jasmine (nāgakesara), bilva fruit, various grains, firewood, and other such materials.

If one performs rites of subjugation, one should perform homa using red and white mustard seeds, blood, mustard oil, poison, bone ash, hair, thorns, *kubjaka* wood, *khadira* wood, *kadara* wood, and wood from thorny trees.
Regarding these three types of homa rites, even if they are not mentioned in the specific root manual (*mūla-vidhi*), one should follow this method.

Next, the ācārya should examine the disciple; if he is a fit vessel for the Dharma and worthy of consecration, the ācārya shall then bestow the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) upon him in accordance with the ritual.

The disciple should first receive empowerment, request the *ācārya* [to perform the rite], and offer a gift. First, one should prepare a new, pure seat; having consecrated that seat by reciting the *vyavasthāna-mantra*, it should be placed within the empowerment maṇḍala.

Furthermore, prepare a new, clean, white parasol; suspend a flower garland above it, and additionally hang white silk banners. Then, recite the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord over the flowers and other offerings.

Furthermore, having placed various auspicious implements within the maṇḍala, the ācārya and his disciple shall protect themselves according to the ritual and cause [the disciple] to sit in its center.
"The ācārya should mix cow's ghee with incense and, reciting the mantra of Kuṇḍalī over it, fumigate the disciple; he should then place the parasol directly above him."

Furthermore, he had other persons hold a pure yak-tail whisk, a fan, and an incense burner; he placed the robes inside a chest, along with conch shells, sinews, and various auspicious objects, and had them hold that chest; he also had them hold a bowl of curd, and in this manner, he had people hold all such items.
If one has attained proficiency, one should produce sounds and hold four vases, keeping them stationed at the sides, while the ācārya recites auspicious and sublime gāthās.
Thus, the sequence has been briefly explained for now; if one wishes to perform it extensively, one should follow the original ritual manual.

The ācārya should universally prostrate to all the deities within the maṇḍala and, with sincere devotion, make a formal request for the sake of the empowerment. He should then take up the flask that was previously recited over one hundred times and slowly circumambulate the maṇḍala.

Having circumambulated it three times, he should again recite the three kinds of mantras over the flask, perform the mudrā upon its crown, and while reciting the root mantra, further recite this mantra to confer empowerment upon him.
If performing the empowerment for the transmission of the Dharma, one should sit facing west;
if performing the empowerment for the pacification of calamities, one should sit facing north;
if performing the empowerment for increase and prosperity, one should sit facing east.
If performing the consecration for subjugation (*abhicāra*), one should sit facing south.

Once the consecration is completed, the preceptor (*ācārya*) next takes hold of the disciple’s garment with his own hand and gives it to him to wear; he likewise applies fragrant unguents to the disciple’s body, presents offerings such as flowers, entwines flower garlands around both shoulders, and further provides armlets to be worn on his wrists.
The ācārya takes the parasol with his own hand and causes the disciple to circumambulate the maṇḍala.
Having completed three circumambulations, he likewise proceeds to the western gate and performs prostrations; meanwhile, the parasol follows him back and forth, shading his head.
The Ācārya petitions the deities, speaking as follows:
"I, [Name], having completed the consecration for [Name], now entrusts them to the deities so that they may uphold the Vidyādhara-piṭaka."
Having spoken these words, he should cause [the disciple] to set aside his parasol and rise; then, facing the maṇḍala, he should recite the samaya precepts for him:
"You have now become a maṇḍala-ācārya and a holder of the vidyā-piṭaka; all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, lords of mantras, and all devas already know you."
"If one sees someone who is fit to be a vessel for the Dharma, out of compassion for them, one should construct a maṇḍala for them and instruct them in the recitation of mantras.
The ācārya should then perform homa for them according to the previously described ritual procedures.
Once the fire has been kindled, perform one hundred *homa* offerings of cow’s ghee using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord;
then, with the mantra of Peace (*śānti*), perform one hundred *homa* offerings of ghee, honey, curd, and rice mixed together;
and finally, perform one hundred *homa* offerings of sesame seeds.
Having performed this, one should pour pure water over the crown of his head.

Next, one should cause him to view the maṇḍala in detail and explain the various deities; one should teach him to observe the characteristics of their respective hand-seals (mudrās) and further instruct him in the mantras of the vidyārājas. Then, one should instruct him to sit in one place and recite the mantra he has received, and subsequently instruct him to make offerings of various incenses and flowers to the primary deity as well as to the other deities.

"Next, the disciple shall prostrate with a sincere heart before the ācārya at the site of the homa. He should offer whatever is required for his needs, or give away all that he possesses—namely, himself, his retinue, his wife and children, his wealth and property—or he should give whatever the ācārya finds pleasing, or whatever he himself holds dear."
If one is poor, one should serve with one's own labor to bring joy to the Honored One; for among all forms of giving, service is supreme.
"Whenever one wishes to practice generosity, one should first offer two pieces of clothing, and only thereafter give away other things; seeking accomplishment, one should give in this manner."

If one seeks samaya, one should give away clothing, gold, cows with their calves, and whatever personal belongings one possesses; even one's own body should be given. One who seeks samaya should practice giving in this manner.
The ācārya then instructs the disciples to sit in order, personally reciting the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* for them to hear.
Next, he expounds the samaya precepts to them all:

"From this day forward, you must always venerate and make offerings to the Triple Gem, as well as to the bodhisattvas and the deities of the mantras, and maintain a constant, superior resolve toward the Mahāyāna sūtras."
Whenever one sees any of the Three Jewels, as well as those who have received the samaya vows, one should give rise to love and joy.
One should always maintain reverence toward the Venerable Ones and must not harbor anger or disdain toward the various devas; rather, one should offer them worship.

One should not place faith in or study the teachings of outsiders; rather, one should give whatever is requested to those who come seeking, constantly arouse compassion for all sentient beings, and diligently seek to cultivate all virtuous qualities.
Always delighting in the Mahāyāna, one should constantly apply diligent effort to the practices of the Vidyā-piṭaka;
while reciting mantras, regarding all secret dharmas within the scriptures of the Vidyā-piṭaka, one must not explain the mantras or mudrās to those who lack the samaya.
"Being endowed with the treasury of learning and clarity, you shall secretly protect and uphold [this].
Having thus spoken the samaya, each [disciple] should be shown the fundamental mudrā they have received and the family (kula) to which their mantra belongs, as well as their fundamental maṇḍala.
"Next, the Ācārya should sprinkle himself with water and again offer arghya to the various deities, making offerings to each deity one by one in sequence.

Next, he should perform homa one hundred and eight times using the mantra of the Maṇḍala Lord; then, perform homa one hundred and eight times using the Śānti mantra; next, perform homa twenty-one times using the Family Heart (Kulahr̥daya) mantra; then, for each individual deity, perform homa seven times each using cow’s ghee and their respective mantras; finally, perform homa as desired using the specific mantra he maintains."
Next, further protect the body according to the ritual and perform offerings to the various directions.

Once the offerings are complete, first wash your hands and sprinkle water for purification upon yourself and your disciples. Then, with incense, flowers, and other items, successively make offerings to and prostrate before all the honored deities. Whatever offerings have been set out should be presented with a sincere heart; only then may they be utilized.
"In all cases where one performs the rites of a maṇḍala, it is essential that one first thoroughly mature one's understanding and achieve clear comprehension before proceeding.
Regarding the maṇḍala rites, one should keep the sūtra at hand and consult the original text repeatedly for fear of errors; how then can one be said not to have matured [one's knowledge]?"
"When constructing a maṇḍala, one must have an assistant for accomplishment guard the site.
Whenever one goes outside, the assistant should enter the location first to provide protection, ensuring it is never left empty.
If there is no such disciple capable of holding the cord, then first drive in one end of the peg, hold it oneself, and mark out the boundary lines."
If there is no assistant to accomplish the task, one must perform all matters oneself.

As for an assistant, if they have an illness, lack moral discipline, are not pure, or are ignorant of the various matters—even if they understand the scriptural collections—they should not be employed.

"If, after the maṇḍala has been completed, there should suddenly appear one born of a noble family among the non-Buddhists (tīrthika), whose mental conduct is gentle and wholesome, who possesses power and integrity, and who possesses deep faith and longing—coming of their own accord with joyful aspiration to enter the maṇḍala—the ācārya, knowing that such a person has faith, shall, even though the construction of the maṇḍala is already finished, cause that person to enter the True Dharma; at that time, he shall perform the rite of summoning for them and invite them to enter the maṇḍala."
If his disciples lack their fundamental auspicious marks or are deficient in the Dharma, they should perform the *śāntika* (pacifying) homa.

If constructing a maṇḍala, one should first petition the king for permission; then, from among the king’s subjects, one should recruit warriors who possess great majesty and each hold weapons, standing around the maṇḍala with fearless hearts. Alternatively, there may be such disciples as are capable vessels for the Dharma who can receive and uphold [the teachings].
"When summoning a disciple, if they are not present, one should fashion their likeness and perform the rites of summoning and so forth;
or if a disciple is intended for consecration but is absent, one should provide another disciple to fulfill the required number for the consecration;
or if a disciple wishes to seek out a specific practice for upholding, if they are absent, one must not substitute another person in place of that disciple."
If, while receiving and upholding [the teachings] for a disciple, one suddenly fails to arrive, it should be known that the ācārya has contracted a grave illness, even unto death.

If, after performing the ritual of invocation, such circumstances arise, one should prepare the maṇḍala on the second day; on that day, one should perform the pacifying homa (śānti-homa), and having again performed the invocation until evening, one prepares the maṇḍala on the third day.
"If, while the maṇḍala is being correctly constructed, some minor implements should suddenly be missing, one need not wait for them; otherwise, if the time passes, various obstacles will arise."
"If difficulties arise while constructing a maṇḍala, one should dispel them with mantras or employ skillful means to pacify the calamities.

If they cannot be removed, one should purify all the ritual implements by sprinkling them with water, perform the offerings and the *argha* offering for the dismissal of the deities all at once, and then perform a pacifying homa on another day; it may also be performed subsequently."

"As for the maṇḍala of the seven vidyārājñīs, one should construct seven enclosures and arrange them according to their respective original rites; do not doubt that those rites and this rite are contradictory.
The ritual for the yakṣa maṇḍala is likewise."
"In some cases, there may be a deficiency in the fundamental ritual (mūla-vidhi) for a maṇḍala; in such instances, one should construct the maṇḍala according to this [present] method.
In other cases, a particular maṇḍala may specifically refer to another method; in those cases, one should again construct the maṇḍala according to that [other] method.

Furthermore, there may be a fundamental ritual that, while mentioning a 'maṇḍala,' does not specify the sequence of its construction; in such cases, one should generally perform it according to the sequence provided by this [present] method."

Just as the maṇḍala rites are extensively explained in the Vidyādhara-piṭaka, or as the maṇḍala is explained according to the specific root-text, or as the maṇḍala is explained through the instructions of the ācārya—following such stated sequences, one should construct the maṇḍala in reliance upon those respective methods; do not give rise to doubt.

"If there is an original ritual manual (*mūla-vidhi*) that prescribes the dimensions of the vase as either large or small, one may nevertheless establish the dimensions according to this [present] method; even if it contradicts the original manual, there is no fault. Furthermore, if one wishes to add offerings for other deities, there is likewise no hindrance."
In all matters concerning the teachings as they have been explained, one must not suppress them by adding superfluous elements, nor should anything be omitted that would render the rite incomplete.

"If there are such mandalas described as having the disciples each take incense burners and lamps to circumambulate the mandala, such extraordinary methods must certainly not be contravened; rather, one should act in accordance with them."
There may be such a maṇḍala rite wherein, when proclaiming the samaya, one says these words:
"You have now boarded the Dharma-ship and shall emerge from saṃsāra."
"Those who scatter flowers with a sincere heart must rely on that teaching and may not contravene it.
Such diverse dharmas as these should each be performed according to their respective original methods; if they are not so prescribed, one must certainly not perform them."
"Upon entering a maṇḍala, there are necessarily four kinds of consecrations (*abhiṣeka*):

first, the removal of obstacles; second, the accomplishment [of rites]; third, the enhancement of one's own person; and fourth, the attainment of the rank of ācārya. These methods of consecration have already been explained at length above."
"Next, the empowerment of the transmission of the vidyā shall now be conferred:
for whichever vidyā one has obtained upon entering the maṇḍala and desires to accomplish, one should recite its mantra over that flask three hundred times and then bestow the empowerment upon them."

Again, using those same substances for the homa as protected by that mantra, recite it seven times; then perform one homa offering, and likewise up to three homa offerings. This is called the second initiation of receiving the vidyā.
If one is afflicted by calamities and receives an empowerment for the purpose of eliminating those calamities, this is called the "empowerment for removing calamities" (*āpattivimocana-abhiṣeka*).

If one receives an empowerment for the sake of seeking peace and happiness, as well as wealth and status, and for the sake of seeking male or female offspring and removing inauspiciousness, this is called the "empowerment for augmentation" (*puṣṭi-abhiṣeka*).

"Whoever receives this empowerment shall be witnessed, blessed, and protected by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and honored deities, as well as by the Bodhisattvas who uphold the mantra practices. All mantras of the Noble Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi shall be fully accomplished; no celestial deities shall be able to cause harm, and they shall all show reverence. One shall not fall into the evil realms within saṃsāra, nor be born into a poor family or among those who are deficient or despised. One shall constantly remember past lives, possess abundant wealth, be endowed with precepts and physical excellence, and be reborn among gods and humans. One shall always encounter the era of a Buddha, never retreat from the bodhicitta, and offer gifts to the honored deities while requesting their joy."

"Furthermore, holding the *argha* offering, one should respectively dismiss [the deities] according to the ritual using their respective root mantras, or perform the dismissal according to the specific rite of the particular *sādhana*. All ritual implements should be cast into a great river; food and drink should be given to poor children, but they should not be given to dogs, crows, or other such lowly birds."
"Whatever wealth and materials are present within the maṇḍala, the ācārya should collect them all and enjoy them as he pleases; he must not give them further to his disciples."
If his disciples were to use these items, they would fall into a breach of their samaya.
Therefore, these items shall be used by the ācārya;
if the ācārya does not use them, they should be offered to the Triple Gem—specifically, items such as the parasol and the yak-tail whisk (camara) should be offered to the Buddha.
Items such as seats, ointments, and incense should be offered to the Dharma;
items such as robes, vases, and utensils should be offered to the Saṃgha.
If there is no Saṃgha, they should be offered to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās—the disciples, down to even the smallest portion, must not use them.
"On the second day, in order to fulfill the deficient dharmas and pacify calamities, perform one hundred and eight *homā* offerings.
11. Chapter Eleven: Supplementing Deficiencies. "Next, it is further explained as before; the method for not omitting anything is not [explicitly] stated."

Regarding those matters not yet explained in the various maṇḍala rites: the ācārya must be well-versed in the vidyā-piṭaka and mantras, possess pure precepts, be endowed with compassion, and be skilled in the art of painting maṇḍalas.
One whose mind is upright and pure should construct a maṇḍala; or, having thoroughly purified and leveled a wide area on the roof of a house, one may also construct it by coating it with white earth;
or one may construct it in a temple;
or, having spread clean wooden planks over water and treated them according to the ritual rules, one may construct it upon them.
As for the maṇḍalas of Jālanātha and Dundubhisvara, they should be constructed upon water;
furthermore, the sites used for Brahminic sacrifices and those used for discarding filth, as well as the grounds where maṇḍalas were previously constructed, should all be abandoned.
Alternatively, it is said that if one constructs a maṇḍala using only a single mantra, one should do so according to that specific rite; this refers precisely to the maṇḍala of the Honored One Tārā.

"If there is one who possesses such a maṇḍala complete with its own retinue of mantras, they should perform it according to that very rite; this refers specifically to the Maṇḍala of the Wrathful Fire Lord (Krodhāgnirāja)."
"If there should be such a maṇḍala for which the mantras of its fundamental rite are incomplete, one should take the universal mantra of the general dharma and construct the maṇḍala."

As for those who employ the mantras and maṇḍalas, they must first recite each one a full thousand times; possessing great merit and virtue, they will before long transcend the ocean of suffering of birth and death and shall attain the fruit of unsurpassed bodhi.
Regarding those who have received empowerment, they possess such immeasurable merits as these, belong to the families of mantras, and practice the bodhisattva path.
Therefore, the ācārya should understand the entire dharma and obtain the permission of empowerment to transmit the teachings; only then should he perform the maṇḍala rites.
If one constructs a maṇḍala in violation of this dharma, it will not be accomplished; upon death, one will fall into hell.

Those who enter such [a maṇḍala] gain no benefit; indeed, it is not merely that there is no benefit, but various obstacles and difficulties arise—namely, famine, pestilence, drought, the rising of bandits, kings waging war against one another, the disciples being harmed by māras, and the ācārya certainly meeting his death. If one constructs a maṇḍala without following the dharma, such various difficulties as these will arise.
"If one receives empowerment within the Buddha Family Maṇḍala, one thereby becomes an ācārya within the maṇḍalas of all three families;
if one receives empowerment within the Avalokiteśvara Maṇḍala, one thereby becomes an ācārya within the maṇḍalas of two families;
and if one receives empowerment within the Vajradhara Family, one thereby becomes an ācārya within the maṇḍalas of one family as well as those of the Mātṛkā deities."

"When constructing a great maṇḍala, one should confer the ācārya-abhiṣeka upon only a single person; for the remaining abhiṣekas, whether three or five, they must never be conferred as pairs, but each must be performed with individual ritual implements."
Those who have received the empowerment of clear illumination (*vidyābhiṣeka*) should be instructed in the methods for accomplishing the maṇḍala;
those who have received other empowerments should be instructed in the fundamental mantras and mudrā methods obtained therein.

"If there is a foolish person who does not enter the maṇḍala, even if they recite the mantra until the full number of repetitions is reached, they will never achieve accomplishment; furthermore, if they give rise to wrong views, that person, upon the end of life, will fall into hell.
If there is someone who bestows the dharma of that mantra upon such a person, they too will fall from the samaya precepts and, after the end of life, fall into the Lohakumbha hell."

If, due to loss of mindfulness or negligence, one falls from the samaya, one should immediately recite the heart-mantra of the respective family one hundred thousand times (*lakṣa*), or recite the Analamūlāni-dhāraṇī one thousand times, or perform a pacifying *homa*, or else enter the great maṇḍala once again.

If there is a foolish person who, not understanding the teachings, constructs a maṇḍala, they will likewise fall into the same place as one who has committed the five heinous crimes of immediate retribution.
"If there are those who, seeking merit in accordance with the Dharma, construct a maṇḍala, those great bodhisattvas will be born in a pure land.

Those who enter that maṇḍala shall not be possessed by malevolent spirits, nor shall they be harmed by various poisons, piśācas, mahoragas, rākṣasas, various kinnaras, or any demonic obstacles; all their karmic hindrances will be completely extinguished, they shall not fall into the evil realms, and the mantras they recite will all achieve accomplishment, such that before long they will attain the fruit of Bodhi."
“Out of compassion, that ācārya should diligently instruct one disciple so that they thoroughly understand the entire ritual system (sarva-dharma) and cause them to uphold my treasury of vidyās.
I have now explained the entire ritual system for all maṇḍalas; whoever constructs a maṇḍala must do so in accordance with this dharma.”

If one is to bestow this Dharma upon a disciple, one must first instruct them in the mantras, mudrās, and mahāmudrās of the Vidyārāja, as well as the various maṇḍalas; only thereafter should one grant this secret Dharma.
The *Rucirā-sūtra*, Volume Lower, concludes here. At the end of the Lingyun (Lingyun) collated edition, it states:
"On the evening of the tenth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Jōkyō era, the first collation was completed by Jōgen, age forty-eight."
